name: Central Sama
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Pallesen, A. Kemp & Craig Soderberg. 2012. Central Sama. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 42(3): 353-359 (Illustrations of the IPA). doi:10.1017/S0025100312000229. Cross-checked: James, Jeremiah Joy. 2017. Central Sinama Voice: A Symmetrical Analysis. MA thesis, GIAL, Dallas, sec. 1.9.2 p.20.
catalog_locator: p.357 section 'Stress' and example table at top of p.358; long-vowel analysis p.357 'Vowels'. James 2017: sec. 1.9.2 p.20.
catalog_quote: Primary stress in Central Sama is not phonemic and falls on the penultimate syllable. When a stem is suffixed, the primary stress shifts so that penultimate stress is maintained, as in the examples below. In words of four syllables or more, secondary stress falls on the syllable two syllables prior to the penultimate. In this section of the paper and in the phonetic transcription which follows, primary stress is marked with [ˈ] while secondary stress is marked with [ˌ]. ... [ˈanäk̚] ‘child’ [äˈnakbɪ] ‘your (plural) child’ [käˈlitän] ‘shark’ [ˌkälɪˈtanän] ‘shark-infested’ [ˈbaɣɪd] ‘matches’ [bäˈɣidnä] ‘his matches’ [ˈbaseʔ] ‘wet’ [mägˌbäseˈʔanän] ‘getting wet’ ... [p.357, Vowels:] All vowels except /ə/ have a lengthened counterpart. We interpret these as sequences of two syllabic vowels because minimal and near-minimal pairs show a semantic contrast between lengthened and unlengthened vowels. Examples: ... [äˈtaː] /ataa/ atā ‘distant’ [ˈatä] /ata/ ata ‘slave’ [sɪˈɣaː] /sigaa/ sigā ‘they (two)’ [ˈsiɣä] /siga/ siga ‘cigarette’
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.citation: Pallesen, A. Kemp & Craig Soderberg. 2012. Central Sama. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 42(3): 353-359 (Illustrations of the IPA). doi:10.1017/S0025100312000229
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (7 pp., text, Cambridge Core open-access download stamp on every page). p.5 = printed p.357, heading 'Stress', reads exactly: 'Primary stress in Central Sama is not phonemic and falls on the penultimate syllable. When a stem is suffixed, the primary stress shifts so that penultimate stress is maintained, as in the examples below. In words of four syllables or more, secondary stress falls on the syllable two syllables prior to the penultimate.' The example table at the top of printed p.358 matches the quoted forms one for one ([ˈanäk̚] 'child', [äˈnakbɪ] 'your (plural) child', [käˈlitän] 'shark', [ˌkälɪˈtanän] 'shark-infested', [ˈbaɣɪd] 'matches', [bäˈɣidnä] 'his matches', [ˈbaseʔ] 'w…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls on the penultimate syllable of the word including suffixes and enclitic pronouns (stress moves rightward under suffixation to stay penultimate). Long (geminate) vowels count as two syllabic vowels, so a word-final long vowel carries the stress (e.g. [äˈtaː] /ataa/ 'distant' vs [ˈatä] /ata/ 'slave'), which James 2017:20 states explicitly: 'The presence of a long vowel in the ultima causes the stress to shift to the right.. thus the stress always falls on the penultimate syllable.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: In words of four or more syllables, secondary stress falls two syllables before the penult (i.e. alternating leftward: [ˌkälɪˈtanän], [mägˌbäseˈʔanän]).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions in the JIPA text; surface-final stress on word-final long vowels follows from the two-vowel analysis (James 2017:20 makes this explicit); James 2017:20 also notes word-initial schwa elision leaves a stressed syllabic nasal ([ˈm̩bal] 'no'). Pallesen 1985:94 notes the only Sama-Bajaw deviation is in Sabah Land Bajaw (NB: schwa penult -> ultima), not in Central Sinama.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word including suffixes and enclitic pronouns ([äˈnakbɪ] 'your child', [bäˈɣidnä] 'his matches'); Pallesen 1985:94 says the rule 'applies to words, not merely to stems'. Illustration speaker from Siasi, Sulu (Central Sinama); James 2017 describes the Sinama Dilaut dialect and agrees.
new_statements.identity_note: The JIPA Illustration's speaker is from Siasi, Sulu Province (Central Sinama, sml = Glottolog cent2092); James 2017 describes the Sinama Dilaut (Sama Dilaut / 'Badjao') dialect of Central Sinama; Pallesen 1985's stress examples are labelled CS.2 = Sama Dilaut (Central Sulu). All three are Central Sama proper, not Southern (sout2918), Northern/Balangingi (bala1311) or Pangutaran Sama. Pallesen 1985 is held held by the project under the sibling directory, not re-downloaded.

tone_statements.quote: No SB language shows the phonemic vowel length distinction in penultimate syllables characteristic of Philippine languages. Rather, most SB languages have been described as having a right-aligned trochaic, stress pattern. Some varieties, such as Pangutaran Sama, have been further described as having iterative secondary stress preceding the primary stress on the penultimate syllable (Pallesen 1979:192). The stress window includes suffixes and genitive pronominal enclitics, as shown in (2).

sources.citation: James, Jeremiah Joy. 2017. Central Sinama Voice: A Symmetrical Analysis. MA thesis, Graduate Institute of Applied Linguistics, Dallas. xv+118 pp.
sources.note: sec. 1.9.2 'Gemination and stress', p.20: 'Stress in Sinama is not contrastive, falling always on the penultimate syllable. The presence of a long vowel in the ultima causes the stress to shift to the right.. A geminate vowel is equivalent to two syllable segments, and thus the stress always falls on the penultimate syllable.' Word-initial schwa elides and the following syllabic consonant carries stress ([ˈm̩bal] 'no'). Sinama Dilaut dialect emphasized; phonology section draws on Pallesen & Soderberg 2012.

sources.note: sec. 3.5 STRESS, printed p.94 (p.124): Proto-Sama-Bajaw penultimate stress 'reconstructed on the basis of its reflex on the penult in all SB languages except in predictable environments in NB'; applies to words not stems, so suffixation shifts stress rightward; examples from CS.2 = Sama Dilaut (Central Sulu, i.e. Central Sinama): bónoq 'to kill', amónoq, bonóqun, pagbonóqbi, pagbonoqánbi. sec. 5.1.3, printed p.164 (p.194): 'Predictable word stress is a feature of all SB daughter languages including AB'. Comparative work, but the CS.2 data are the author's own field language.

sources.note: Section 2 'Phonology' has no mention of tone, pitch or pitch accent anywhere in the chapter. Word prosody is described as stress: no phonemic penultimate vowel length (unlike Philippine languages); most Sama-Bajaw languages have a right-aligned trochaic stress pattern (penultimate primary stress), Pangutaran Sama with iterative secondary stress; the stress window includes suffixes and genitive enclitics (Central Sinama example from Pallesen 1985:94). Also notes pre-tonic (pre-penultimate) vowel neutralization in Sulu varieties.
